cards.title: Your AI Coding Assistant Just Got Dumber: Builders Are Desperate for a 'Control Layer'
cards.thesis: AI development tools like Claude are supposed to make coding easier, but many builders are getting frustrated because these tools are becoming less reliable. They're making mistakes like ignoring instructions or breaking existing code, and even adding unwanted links to projects, leading to a lot of manual cleanup. This means developers need better ways to manage and guide these AI helpers, giving them more control over the AI's output.

evidence.text: Many users feel 'Claude Opus is becoming dumber on complex tasks' since recent updates, citing issues where it 'constantly ignores mandatory project rules, makes unsolicited edits to unrelated files, and breaks working code,' failing to update documentation when code changes.
Developers are frustrated that Claude now automatically appends a private session link to every commit, which doesn't make sense for a public commit history and feels like unnecessary noise.
One user discovered that Claude's advertised '20x usage' was only for a 5-hour window, not a weekly limit, making the pricing feel misleading and causing frustration.
People are having 'a lot of issues using multiple [AI] sessions at once to build things,' struggling to make AI agents stop at certain points or manage complex workflows effectively.
The sentiment that 'you are the harness' for AI means the programmer's skill in guiding and managing AI makes the biggest difference, not just the raw power of the AI model itself.

cards.opportunity: Builders are hitting a wall because tools like Claude are making sloppy mistakes, ignoring rules, and messing up documentation. People aren't just looking for better AI models anymore; they desperately need a 'control layer' that lets them easily review and manage AI-generated code changes, automatically flag documentation that needs updating, and prevent unwanted edits *before* they break things. Ship a simple plug-in for VS Code or Replit that acts like a smart gatekeeper for AI output, giving developers explicit control over what gets committed, and you'll own the frustrated-developer market who's tired of fixing AI's mess.

cards.title: AI Agents Are Hungry for Skills: Your Chance to Build the App Store for AI Superpowers
cards.thesis: People are going all-in on building specific 'skills' for AI agents, which are like pre-packaged capabilities that let AI do very specific tasks. There's a massive demand for these ready-to-use skills, especially when they can work across different AI platforms and fit into complex multi-agent setups (where multiple AIs work together).

evidence.text: This GitHub project, 'scientific-agent-skills,' lets you 'Turn any AI agent into an AI Scientist' with 165 ready-to-use validated skills and 100+ scientific databases. It's used by 190,000+ scientists and works with major AI tools like Cursor, Claude Code, and follows an 'open Agent Skills standard.'
The 'DoubaoWorkGuide' from AlephAITech details how to use a Chinese AI work system, specifically mentioning 'Skills, connectors, automation, and multi-Agent workflows.'

A project called 'Claude2API' acts like a universal translator, letting different AI models (like OpenAI and Anthropic's Claude) talk to each other through one standard connection (an API, which is a way for different software to communicate). It supports various AI clients and features like multi-turn conversations and tool use.
'Wonder-Pill' is a specific 'Claude skill' designed for brainstorming, turning ideas into interactive mind maps of 'inverted assumptions' without giving answers, just provocations.

'SmartOpenMAIC' (Open Multi-Agent Interactive Classroom) promises an immersive, multi-agent learning experience 'in just one click,' highlighting the demand for easy setup of collaborative AI systems.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's building individual 'skills' for AI agents, but the real gold rush is in making these skills discoverable and easily connectable across different AI platforms. Think about building a 'plug-and-play' directory or marketplace for these agent skills, where builders can find validated, domain-specific capabilities (like for science or marketing) and easily integrate them into their own multi-agent workflows. The 'open Agent Skills standard' means you don't even have to build the skills yourself—just make them accessible and interoperable for the thousands of builders looking to give their AIs superpowers.

cards.title: App Stores Are Squeezing Open Source: New Ways to Fund Your Project
cards.thesis: Major app stores like Google Play are cracking down on how independent projects, especially open-source apps, can accept donations. They're blocking direct links to external funding platforms (like Open Collective), forcing developers to either use in-app purchases (where the app store takes a cut) or find completely new ways to get community support.

evidence.text: Google Play is no longer allowing Open Collective donation links for apps like AnkiDroid, directly impacting how open-source projects receive community funding.

A Dropbox data breach occurred due to a vulnerability in a third-party identity provider (a service that verifies user identity), highlighting the risks when relying on external systems for critical functions.

Reddit has made old.reddit.com (the classic user interface) inaccessible to logged-out users, demonstrating how platforms can change rules to control user experience and push adoption of new features.

cards.opportunity: With Google Play just banning direct donation links, open-source projects are desperate for alternative, frictionless ways to get funded without losing 30% to platform fees. Build a simple 'micro-patronage' platform or embeddable widget that lets users easily donate or become members directly, perhaps even with crypto options, and helps projects clearly communicate their value. You could launch a basic version this weekend, connecting Stripe or a crypto wallet to a customizable donation button that app developers can drop into their external links or websites.

cards.title: Everyone's Launching 'Happ' Proxy Clients — What's the Catch (and the Opportunity)?
cards.thesis: Multiple independent projects on GitHub are popping up with almost identical descriptions for 'Happ,' a free cross-platform proxy client. A proxy client is a tool that routes your internet traffic through another server, which helps you hide your location or bypass internet restrictions. This surge suggests a strong, unfulfilled demand for simple, accessible ways to manage internet access, especially for those who need to get around geo-blocks or privacy concerns.

evidence.text: One project, 'PigeonAlembic/happ,' describes itself as 'Happ — a free cross-platform proxy client with Windows support.'
Another project, 'Virtualtaknot/happ-vpn,' uses the exact same description: 'Happ — a free cross-platform proxy client with Windows support.'
A third project, 'PigeonAlembic/happ-vpn,' also states: 'Happ — a free cross-platform proxy client with Windows support.'

cards.opportunity: Everyone's launching 'Happ' as a free proxy client, but the real pain point for most people is trusting a random repo or setting it up themselves. You could build a super simple, one-click installer or even a managed service that lets users securely deploy their own 'Happ' instance on a cheap cloud server. Charge a small monthly fee for the convenience and peace of mind, making it easy for anyone to get their own reliable, private proxy without the tech headache.

cards.title: Discord's Dead in Russia? There's a Hidden Goldmine in Making It Work Again.
cards.thesis: Internet restrictions in Russia are making it tough for people to use Discord, leading to a surge in demand for workaround tools. Developers are creating 'modified builds' of existing censorship bypass software (like Zapret and GoodbyeDPI) to get Discord running stably again, showing a clear, unmet need for reliable access.

evidence.text: A GitHub project with 60 engagements provides a 'Discord fix' — a modified version of Zapret and GoodbyeDPI specifically to bypass Russian government restrictions and ensure stable Discord operation in Russia.
Another GitHub project, with 50 engagements, offers a 'Discord fix' based on Zapret and GoodbyeDPI, designed to circumvent internet censorship in Russia and allow consistent use of Discord.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's downloading these GitHub repos just to get Discord working in Russia, but the setup is a pain and they're always wondering if it's up-to-date. You could build a super simple, one-click installer or a small app that auto-updates these censorship bypass tools, making it dead simple for non-technical users to keep their Discord running without hassle. It's a clear problem with an existing, clunky solution, and the first person to productize a reliable, user-friendly wrapper will own that market.
